turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down there. Your wife is welcome to stay. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this wound, doctor. The appendix operation, ten days ago. It's gone red and there's stuff leaking out of it. I don't know, it's not right at all.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was grand the first week, pottering about. Then it turned.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Open job, was it, or the keyhole?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Open. Scar's down in the right side. Your man in the hospital said it was straightforward enough.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the redness come on?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Two days, I'd say. Maybe. I can't swear to it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three days. Sunday evening the skin around it was pink, and I said it to him.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Was it Sunday? I had it in my head as Monday. I don't know.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two and three days, and ye aren't fully agreed. And the discharge, what's that like?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yellowish, on the dressing. Not a huge amount. There's a smell off it, a small bit. I think. I don't know.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I took the plaster off this morning before we came. It was wet through, yellow.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you get a temperature?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night I was roasting. Whether I have one now, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I put the thermometer on him. I thought thirty-nine, but I had it wrong. It was 38.6. He seems cooler this morning, I'd say.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shivers with that, or just the heat?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Shivery last night, yeah. Not so much today.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting? Diarrhoea?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. No diarrhoea. The bowels are a bit slow, that's all.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waterworks? Burning when you pass water?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's grand. Not a bother.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the wound sore, or is it just the look of it?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): It's sore, worse when I get up and move. I take the white pain tablets. Five hundred milligrams... no, sorry, I take two, so a thousand milligrams, four times a day. They take the edge off.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol. The plain ones from the chemist. He's been good with those.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did they send you home on an antibiotic?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The big white ones. Augmentin, that's what the chemist said. They were five hundred milligrams. I was on them five days... or was it seven. I don't know, doctor. I finished the box anyway.

[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said seven days, three times a day. The box was empty after five. He might have been doubling up, I couldn't tell you. He told me they were five hundred, but the packet said six hundred and twenty-five.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): And the strong pain ones, the codeine, I stopped them. After two days. They bunged me up completely.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the lactulose, the syrup for the bowels? Did you take any of that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I never took it. It's sitting in the press at home. I don't know, I just didn't.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Separate to all that, he uses the purple inhaler for his asthma. Most mornings.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the purple one. Asthma since I was a teenager. It's been quiet, not a bother.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand, so the asthma is there in the background and not flaring. Any drug allergies I should know about, penicillin especially?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Nothing I can think of. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother has always said he came out in a rash with penicillin when he was small. He's stayed away from it since. He has no memory of it himself.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember any rash. I don't know what she's on about.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. I'm not going to stamp that as a definite allergy, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't there either. We'll keep you off penicillin today and think about what else would cover a wound like this.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me get this dressing off and have a proper look. There's redness a couple of centimetres all around the wound in the right lower side, and yellow discharge at the bottom end. It's tender, the stitches are still in, and there's no fluctuance, no pocket I can feel under the skin.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is ninety-two. Blood pressure one twenty-eight over seventy-eight. You feel a bit warm to the hand, even if we haven't a fresh temperature here.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it infected? I don't know what I'm meant to do.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd say this is a superficial wound infection. That's where I'm landing for now. It might be a stitch abscess, and I can't fully rule out a deeper little collection, so I won't conclude that part yet. I'm not calling it an abscess on today's look alone.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the tablets change, then?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): They will. Whatever way the Augmentin days fell, that course is finished and the wound has come up after it. I won't use co-amoxiclav or flucloxacillin with that penicillin story hanging over us. I'll start clarithromycin, five hundred milligrams, twice a day, by mouth, for seven days.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is that the yellow box one? I always mix the colours up.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't mind the colour of the box. It's clarithromycin. Finish the seven days even if the wound looks quieter on day three.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And I keep taking the white ones?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the paracetamol at a gram four times a day. Leave the codeine off unless the pain is desperate, it was slowing the bowel.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send a wound swab. If the lab comes back with something the clarithromycin doesn't cover, we might switch, but only if the result says so. I won't guess that today.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Are you doing bloods? I hate the needle, but I don't know if you need them.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If you're worse when I see you again we might send a CRP and a full blood count. I won't order them now.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Do I keep dressing it at home the way the ward showed me?

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Fresh dressing once a day, keep it clean and dry, no soaking in the bath. If the redness starts racing outwards, or the fever comes back, or the wound opens, go to the emergency department. Don't sit on that.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): When am I back? And I don't know about the van. I'm meant to be working.
[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He drives a delivery van. He's been off since the operation.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay off the driving another few days at least, until this is quieter. I'll see you back here in two days. That's booked, not a maybe. We'll look at the wound again, and the swab if it's through.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days, grand. I still don't know about the penicillin, doctor. It's all news to me.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll ring his mother this evening and ask her straight. If she remembers a proper reaction I'll call the surgery.

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would settle it better than we can today. For now we treat penicillin as a possible problem and avoid it. Take the clarithromycin with food if it turns your stomach. I'll see you in two days.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
